Front Matter · Teacher Resources
Teacher’s Manual
Grade 7 Texas History · Second Semester (Weeks 19–36)
📖 WHAT THIS COURSE COVERS AND WHY IT IS ORGANIZED THIS WAY

This build covers the second semester: Quarter 3 (“The Price of Union,” Weeks 19–27) and Quarter 4 (“Convergence and Divergence,” Weeks 28–36). The first semester (Weeks 1–18, Spanish Texas through annexation) is a separate build. The semester is organized around one governing question, stated to students in the Week 36 essay: What does it cost Texas to belong to America, and what, even so, stays distinctly Texan? Every week’s content is chosen to build toward an answer to that question, not to march through a checklist of standards.

The Spring Comprehensive Course Map (in this course’s build folder, not reproduced here) is the authoritative document for narrative, sequencing, and pacing. It is finished and not open to restructuring. TEKS benchmarks are cited against the lessons that already carry them; they never drive adding units, reordering weeks, or reshaping content to chase coverage. See the Standards Alignment Matrix for where each benchmark lands.

🎯 THE HISTORIOGRAPHICAL APPROACH

The course does not present history as a march toward inevitable progress, nor as material conditions alone determining outcomes. It leans on historical contingency (the Civil War’s outcome, the border war, and the end of Reconstruction each had plausible alternate paths) and a Classical Republican evaluation of regimes and leaders: a people’s laws, customs, and character help explain why some political communities succeed and others fail at the first-order problems of internal peace and external defense. The narrative spine is Great Men and Great Events: this is the history of one political community, and its existence depended on real military and political outcomes. Antagonists are treated by the same standard as protagonists, with their strengths and failings both carrying explanatory weight.

Editorial rule for lessons. Tell what happened, who did it, and why, and where it helps what might have gone differently. No retrospective moral commentary and no instructions to students about how to weigh the story.

💪 THE VIRTUE THREAD

Optima’s seven virtues (courage, courtesy, honesty, perseverance, self-government, service, responsibility) are attached to the people in the story, never to what the student does, and only where the week’s content supports it. Quarter 3’s throughline is responsibility (what union costs and who carries the bill while a people learns to govern itself). Quarter 4’s throughline is service (the Alliance’s cooperation, wartime mobilization, civil rights litigants, and the question of what service to Texas itself still means).

The weekly mapping is a proposal grounded in the map’s content, not a fixed doctrine. Week 35 may be revisited.

⚠️ PACING PRESSURE POINTS

Week 21 carries the Civil War and Reconstruction in one week, much tighter than the first semester’s three weeks on the Texas Revolution. The course map leaves open whether it needs more room. Do not resolve it by moving content; ask the course lead.

Weeks 22 and 23 are dense: four lessons carry TEKS 7.13 through 7.17, with four civics primary sources.

Reading length. Every lesson reads inside the 800–1,200 word range except Week 19 Lesson 2, which runs long (about 1,370 words) because it covers Scott’s campaign, the treaty, and the Compromise of 1850.

📄 PRIMARY SOURCE STATUS

The map names two sources per week (one for Week 36). Public-domain texts only were used. Where the named document could not be located or was in copyright, a stated substitute was used or the item is flagged.

Substituted: Week 23 (Jordan’s 1974 impeachment statement for the 1976 keynote, because of rights); Week 25 (Cortína’s 1859 proclamation for the Ranger muster roll); Week 30 (Governor Sterling’s 1931 martial-law proclamation for a roughneck account); Week 32 (the Doris Miller Navy Cross citation for a serviceman’s letter); Week 35 (Bush 1995 inaugural for a realignment document).

Not found, so each of these weeks has one source ready and one missing: Weeks 23 (Rayburn), 24 (a Ranger account), 25 (a German immigrant diary), 26 (a Red River War report), 27 (a barbed-wire advertisement), 28 (McCallum), 30 (Dallas bank material), 31 (a WPA report), 34 (both sources, because the candidates are in copyright). Week 34’s primary source assignment is not built yet.

Each primary source assessment has exactly two questions, written to work with the source that is ready.

📊 HOW A WEEK IS BUILT

Every week contains two lesson pages (hosted on GitHub Pages and embedded in Canvas by iframe; each lesson carries two ungraded interactive activities, a read-aloud player at the top, and a pronunciation button on every glossary entry), a Module Map page, one reading quiz (6 to 7 inference-based questions, two attempts, highest score kept), and one primary source assessment (exactly two questions, scored on the shared three-criterion, 16-point rubric (Understanding 6, Reasoning 6, Clarity 4), typed in Canvas). Each week module also opens with an ungraded Module Intro survey (the week’s essential question as a first answer) and closes with an ungraded Module Outro survey (the question revisited, a confidence rating, what is still unclear, and a virtue reflection), so the teacher can read responses across the whole class. Week 34’s two sources are Texas Senate resolutions (SR 118 of 2017 and SR 99 of 1997), substituted for the map’s early-1980s and 1970s sources, which are in copyright. A VR write-up paired to the week’s immersive session is planned for every week and is not built yet.

Quarter exams. The Quarter 3 Capstone (a five-paragraph essay of about 500 words, 16 points, with a fixed prompt) and the Quarter 3 Exam (30 multiple-choice questions) sit in Week 27, and the Quarter 4 Exam (28 questions) at Week 36, each exam covering only its own quarter. The Q3 Capstone prompt is fixed and should not be rewritten: Annexation settled who would own Texas, but not what belonging to the Union would require. Using at least three pieces of evidence from the quarter, explain what Texas had to settle after 1845, and how each thing was settled. A Spring-only Year-End Synthesis Essay (about 400–500 words) at Week 36 asks how the relationship between Texas and the United States changed between 1846 and today; it does not draw on the first semester. Week 36 has one lesson plus the exam and essay, so its quiz and primary source assessment are attached to Lesson 1. The essay prompt is fixed and should not be rewritten.

🔧 WHAT IS NOT BUILT YET

The VR write-ups for all 18 weeks; the “confirm your submissions” checklists (drafted as files, not yet placed on Canvas pages); and a weighted group for synchronous work, which this On-Demand build does not include (see Start Here: Set Your Weights and Syllabus).

📕 SCOPE NOTE

This course is a full-year, 36-week sequence; this page covers the second semester only (Quarters 3 and 4, Weeks 19–36), from the Rio Grande in 1846 to contemporary Texas. Weeks 1–18 (the first semester) are a separate build. The Comprehensive Course Map in this course’s build folder is the authoritative source for week-level lesson content, working notes, and pacing. This page is a quick-reference index, not a replacement for it.

🧭 THREADS THAT RUN THROUGH THE SEMESTER

The border. The semester opens by settling the Nueces-versus-Rio-Grande question by war (Week 19), returns to the border as the economic seam of NAFTA and the maquiladoras (Week 35), and closes on it in the capstone (Week 36).

The Comanche frontier. Opened in the first semester, it runs under the state-building weeks (19–23) and resolves in Weeks 24–26 with Quanah Parker’s surrender in 1875.

The absorption arc (Weeks 31–33). Radio and the New Deal begin to close the gap between Texas and the nation; World War II completes it; civil rights litigation brings Texas institutions into line with federal constitutional standards. The two “Americanization of Texas” lesson titles (Weeks 32 and 33) echo each other on purpose.

Anchor dates. 1861 (Week 20), 1876 (Week 22), and 1901 (Week 29) are the three dates the TEKS require that the first semester left over, completing all eight across the year.

M365 Setup & File Organization Guide
Pinned reference · read this first if you are new to the course, or joining mid-year
🖥️ SIGNING IN

Go to office.com and sign in with your school Microsoft account (not a personal Microsoft account). You will have access to Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and OneDrive from any device.

📁 THIS COURSE’S ONEDRIVE FOLDER

Create (or confirm you have) the following folder path in OneDrive: Optima → History → TXHIST7_Semester2. Any Word document your teacher asks you to submit for this course is saved here before you submit it in Canvas.

📝 FILE NAMING RULE

Name every file: LastName_FirstName_AssignmentShortName_TXHIST7. Example: Smith_Jane_YearEndEssay_TXHIST7. If an assignment has drafts, add _Draft1, _Draft2; the version you turn in is always labeled _Final.

📤 SUBMITTING VIA CANVAS

Most written work in this course is typed directly into the assignment in Canvas. When an assignment asks for a file, open it in Canvas and use the OneDrive submission tab to attach your file from your course folder, or upload the file if OneDrive cloud assignments are not enabled for this section.

❓ JOINED MID-YEAR?

Confirm you have a school M365 account, create your OneDrive course folder if it does not exist, review the file naming rule above, and bookmark this page. Ask your teacher whether any earlier assignments need to be resubmitted in M365 format.

💬 WHERE TO GET HELP

Your teacher’s office hours (see the Course Syllabus) are the first stop. Microsoft’s own beginner tutorials are at support.microsoft.com.

assignments.title: Week 19 Primary Source Assessment
assignments.html:
Week 19 Primary Source Assessment

Read the sources below. Then answer both questions in 3 to 5 sentences each, in your own words. Use what you learned in the lessons as well as what the source says. Your teacher will score your answers with the rubric on this page.

SOURCE A
President James K. Polk, Special Message to Congress on Mexican Relations, May 11, 1846 (excerpt)

In the meantime, we have tried every effort at reconciliation. The cup of forbearance had been exhausted even before the recent information from the frontier of the Del Norte. But now, after reiterated menaces, Mexico has passed the boundary of the United States, has invaded our territory and shed American blood upon the American soil. She has proclaimed that hostilities have commenced, and that the two nations are now at war.

SOURCE B
Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, February 2, 1848 (excerpts)

Article V. The boundary line between the two Republics shall commence in the Gulf of Mexico, three leagues from land, opposite the mouth of the Rio Grande, otherwise called Rio Bravo del Norte . . .

Article VIII. Mexicans now established in territories previously belonging to Mexico, and which remain for the future within the limits of the United States, as defined by the present treaty, shall be free to continue where they now reside, or to remove at any time to the Mexican Republic, retaining the property which they possess in the said territories . . .

Article XII. In consideration of the extension acquired by the boundaries of the United States, as defined in the fifth article of the present treaty, the Government of the United States engages to pay to that of the Mexican Republic the sum of fifteen millions of dollars.

QUESTION 1

Polk says Mexico shed American blood "upon the American soil." What did Polk assume about the land where the fighting happened, and why would Mexico have disagreed?

QUESTION 2

Article V of the treaty places the boundary at the Rio Grande. Suppose the treaty had instead placed it at the Nueces River. How might that have changed Texas's position, and would Texans have accepted it? Explain your reasoning.

assignments.title: Week 20 Primary Source Assessment
assignments.html:
Week 20 Primary Source Assessment

Read the sources below. Then answer both questions in 3 to 5 sentences each, in your own words. Use what you learned in the lessons as well as what the source says. Your teacher will score your answers with the rubric on this page.

SOURCE A
John C. Calhoun, South Carolina Exposition and Protest, 1828 (excerpt)

[T]o divide power, and to give to one of the parties the exclusive right of judging of the portion allotted to each, is in reality not to divide at all; and to reserve such exclusive right to the general government, (it matters not by what department it be exercised,) is in fact to constitute it one great consolidated government, with unlimited powers, and to reduce the states to mere corporations.

SOURCE B
Sam Houston, protest to the Secession Convention, March 16, 1861 (excerpt)

Fellow-Citizens, in the name of your rights and liberties, which I believe have been trampled upon, I refuse to take this oath. In the name of the nationality of Texas, which has been betrayed by the Convention, I refuse to take this oath. In the name of the Constitution of Texas, I refuse to take this oath. In the name of my own conscience and manhood, which this Convention would degrade by dragging me before it, to pander to the malice of my enemies, I refuse to take this oath. I deny the power of this Convention to speak for Texas . . . I protest . . . against all the acts and doings of this convention and I declare them null and void.

QUESTION 1

Calhoun warns that giving the national government the sole right to judge its own powers would "reduce the states to mere corporations." What idea about the Union is he defending, and how could secession leaders in 1861 use the same idea?

QUESTION 2

Houston refused the oath and said the Convention could not speak for Texas, yet the Convention declared his office empty. Explain why his refusal cost him the governorship even though he believed the Convention had no power.

assignments.title: Week 27 Quarter 3 Capstone
assignments.html:
For nine weeks you have followed what happened after Texas joined the Union. This essay asks you to explain, in your own words and with your own evidence, what Texas had to settle once it belonged to the United States.

The prompt. Annexation settled who would own Texas, but not what belonging to the Union would require. Using at least three pieces of evidence from the quarter, explain what Texas had to settle after 1845, and how each thing was settled.

Directions.
1. Look back over Weeks 19 to 27 and your notes.
2. Choose at least three specific pieces of evidence from at least three different weeks. Evidence can come from any lesson, for example the war with Mexico and the treaty that fixed the border, secession and Reconstruction, the Constitution of 1876, the closing of the Comanche frontier, or the cattle kingdom and the railroads.
3. Write a five-paragraph essay of about 500 words: an opening paragraph that states your claim, three body paragraphs that each develop one piece of evidence, and a closing paragraph that ties them into one explanation.
4. Type your essay in the box below and submit it in Canvas. Use your own words.

Success criteria.
☐ My opening paragraph states a clear claim.
☐ I used at least three pieces of evidence from at least three different weeks.
☐ Each body paragraph names the event, person, or law and explains how it was settled.
☐ My closing paragraph ties the evidence into one explanation.
☐ I wrote it in my own words.

assignments.title: Week 36 Year-End Synthesis Essay
assignments.html:
Between 1846 and today, Texas fought a war with Mexico, left the Union and came back, wrote a new constitution, struck oil, and grew into one of the largest states in the country. Through all of it, Texans and Americans kept settling the same question: what is decided in Austin, and what is decided in Washington?

Write an essay of about 400 to 500 words that answers this question: How did the relationship between Texas and the United States change between 1846 and today?

Your essay should:
1. State your answer in a clear opening sentence.
2. Use at least three specific examples from this semester. Name the event, person, or law, and explain what happened and how it changed the relationship.
3. Use at least one specific example of something Texas kept in its own hands.
4. Close by naming the single event or decision you think mattered most, and say why.

You may draw on any lesson, source, or event from the semester. Use your own words.

Leaving the Union would bring a long war, and Texas would lose it.
The Declaration of Causes was too short to explain the decision.
Texas had no right to join the Confederacy as a new state.

Secession was never put to a popular vote of any kind.
Texans were not all of one mind about secession.

Slavery and the threat to its spread into new land.
A dispute with Mexico over the Río Grande border.
The cost of keeping up the forts along the frontier.

The soldiers wanted to give up the fight and were trying to send Lee home.
The soldiers had stopped obeying every order.
Lee had little experience leading men in battle.

Hood refused to attack at Atlanta, Franklin, or Nashville and was relieved.

Daring that works for a brigade can be dangerous in command of a whole army.

The Union army had built and guarded the road to the river crossing.
Mexico was neutral, so ships of other countries could dock there despite the blockade.
Texas ports had never shipped any cotton before the war began in 1861.

Congress and many Northerners saw the Black Codes as slavery under another name.
Texas had refused to hold any elections after the war.
President Johnson wanted the army to run every state government.

Grant had no soldiers available anywhere in the whole country at the time.
The Freedmen's Bureau had asked Davis to step down from the governor's office.
Davis had lost by a wide margin, and many white Texans would have fought the army.

questions.text: According to the lesson, what did freedpeople do after the Union army announced freedom in Texas?

answers.text: Many searched for family and built churches and schools, though most received no land.
Most were given small farms by the Freedmen's Bureau and soon left cotton farming for good.
Nearly all stayed on the same farms under the same old terms.
Most left Texas at once and crossed the river into Mexico.

answers.text: That Texas had too few courts and judges to settle the disputes among its people.
That a strong governor, like Davis, could misuse his power.
That the federal army would leave Texas unprotected.
That voters would not take part in elections.

answers.text: The governor controls every office in the executive branch.
The legislature chooses each of these officers in turn.
These offices were taken out of the constitution in 1876.

questions.text: Section 1 of the 1876 constitution says Texas is subject to the United States Constitution but also says the Union depends on local self-government. What do the delegates seem to believe?

answers.text: Texas should leave the Union a second time and stand alone again.
The national government in Washington should run all Texas public schools.
Texas belongs in the nation, but Texans must govern themselves at home.
Local governments should be done away with in favor of the state.

questions.text: Why is the Texas Constitution much longer than the U.S. Constitution?

It was written by a very large group of delegates who wanted every state law listed in its text.
Texas needed every state law to be listed inside the constitution.
Congress required Texas to include all of these details in the text.

questions.text: A change to the Texas Constitution requires an amendment approved by voters. What is one result mentioned in the lesson?

answers.text: The constitution has stayed exactly the same since 1876, so no amendment has ever been needed.
The governor can change the constitution alone whenever he sees fit.
Only the legislature votes on each amendment before it becomes law.
Voters have approved hundreds of amendments to keep up with a growing state.

questions.text: The 1876 constitution required separate public schools for white and Black children. What does the lesson suggest about the limits the delegates wrote?

answers.text: They were aimed at the governor, but they did not fall on the governor alone.
They protected Black Texans from losing any of their rights and ended segregation in the public schools.
They ended the segregation of the public schools across Texas.
They applied only to government officials and not to the public.

questions.text: The state itself does not collect a property tax. Which level of government mainly does?

answers.text: The Texas legislature in Austin.
The federal government in Washington.
School districts, cities, and counties.
The Railroad Commission of Texas.

Only people who lived in the Hill Country and near the coast.
Many Black Texans, many Mexican Americans, and many poor white farmers.
Only women, until they won the right to vote in 1919.

questions.text: In much of the 1900s, the Democratic primary often decided who would hold office in Texas. Why did that make the white primary so powerful?

answers.text: Primary elections were against the law in Texas, so only the general election mattered at all.
Republicans always won the Democratic primary by a large margin.
The primary was held only one time in every ten years.
Keeping Black voters out of the primary kept them out of the real contest.

questions.text: In Smith v. Allwright (1944), what did the Supreme Court decide?

answers.text: The Court decided that the poll tax must be ended in every county of the state.
Women could vote in primary elections in Texas.
The voting age should be lowered from 21 to 18.
A party could not keep voters out of a primary because of race.

Rayburn opposed extending the draft and voted against it himself.
Without that vote, the army might have fallen apart before Pearl Harbor.
Texas leaders had very little influence over the decisions made in Washington.

A strong wish to hold office for its own sake and no other.
A refusal to work with anyone who belonged to another party.

answers.text: He is tied to Texas by birth, though he grew up elsewhere.

He was born in a small town in Kansas.
He taught Mexican American children in Cotulla.

There was only one chief who spoke for every band.
A promise made by one band did not bind the other bands.

answers.text: The Comanche gave up hunting bison and began to farm the plains, which kept them near their camps.
The Comanche moved back to the Rocky Mountains and never returned to Texas.
Texans gave the Comanche their first horses in the year 1840 as gifts.
Riders could follow bison for hundreds of miles and strike a ranch before help arrived.

answers.text: It covered only the Penateka and a small area, and other bands were not part of it.
The Germans broke the treaty within a week, and the Comanche then refused to speak with Texans again.
The Comanche had no interest in making any treaty with anyone at all.

answers.text: The forts had all been closed by the army in 1848, so Texans had to defend themselves alone.
The forts were far apart, and soldiers on foot rarely caught Comanche riders.
The Rangers were paid much more than the regular soldiers were.
The Comanche never attacked any settlement that stood near a fort.

answers.text: It could shoot far enough to outrange any rifle then in use, so the Comanche could not get near.
It frightened the Comanche, who had never before seen a gun of any kind.
It was the first firearm that anyone had ever used in the state of Texas.
The Rangers could fire again and again from horseback instead of stopping to reload.

answers.text: How hard it was to tell a camp of warriors from a camp of families.
That the Comanche had given up raiding, and that Rangers never harmed any civilians.
That Rangers always took care to avoid harming civilians.
That the army alone defended the frontier by then.

questions.text: Comancheros traded bread, tools, and cloth for horses and cattle. How did that trade help the Comanche?

answers.text: It forced them to stop raiding Texas ranches and to depend on the traders for food.
It made them depend on Texas merchants for food.
It replaced hunting bison as their main source of food.
It gave them goods and a market for animals, many taken in raids.

He learned his trade only from German settlers.

Vaqueros were forced to leave Mexico by a treaty.
Anglo ranchers relied on vaquero skill and borrowed their methods.
The King Ranch was first a German farming village.

answers.text: They raised no animals of any kind, and lived only on the grain that they grew on their land.
They moved their herds each spring on long drives all the way to Kansas.

He taught the vaqueros how to rope and brand cattle on the range.
He wrote down the stories of old ranch hands so later readers could learn them.
He founded the Texas Rangers in the 1820s with Stephen F. Austin.

answers.text: The Rangers had no horses at all, and could patrol only on foot in the country near the forts.
The frontier was huge, and raiders who knew the ground could move faster than the Rangers.
The raiders had no reason to flee because Rangers never gave chase.
The settlers never reported any thefts to the Rangers or to anyone else.

The treaty of 1848 required Mexico to refuse.
Slavery was against the law in Mexico.
The Rio Grande was not yet a border between the countries.

Cortina wanted Texas to leave the Union and join Mexico in 1859.
Cortina refused to fight at all when he reached the town of Brownsville.

It took the place of the railroads for hauling cattle across the plains.
It pumped water from underground, so ranchers no longer had to stay near a river.

questions.text: A steer sold for a few dollars in Texas and about ten times as much in Northern cities after the Civil War. What does this best explain?

answers.text: Why Texans drove herds north to a railhead, since carrying cattle to market earned a profit.
Why Texans stopped raising cattle altogether when the Civil War came to an end and prices were low.
Why railroads were built across the whole state of Texas well before the war.
Why the Comanche raided the largest ranches in the years after the war.

questions.text: Why did some drives shift west from the Chisholm Trail onto the Western Trail toward Dodge City?

answers.text: The Chisholm Trail ran out of grass for the cattle after one season.
The Red River dried up each summer and could not be crossed.
Kansas, worried about Texas fever, closed more of its land to Texas herds.
Abilene lost its railroad connection when the company moved its tracks away.

questions.text: In the Mason County War, quarrels over cattle led to killings. Which condition of the open range helped cause trouble?

answers.text: Every ranch was fenced in and guarded by armed riders each night, so cattle were never mixed up.
Texas had strict courts that sat in session in every county.
Rangers were stationed at every ranch to guard against cattle thieves.
Cattle wandered and brands were hard to check, so unbranded calves could be claimed by anyone.

questions.text: In 1883 angry cowboys and small ranchers cut fences across Texas in a drought year. What best explains their anger?

answers.text: Fences cut off trails and water holes that had been free to everyone.
Fences made the cattle weaker and slower on the trails north.
The new fences were built of wood and cost far too much.
Ranchers wanted barbed wire banned across the border in neighboring Kansas.

questions.text: Walter Prescott Webb argued that three tools made it possible to settle the dry Great Plains. Which set is correct?

answers.text: The Colt revolver, barbed wire, and the windmill.
The railroad, the telegraph, and the steam engine.
The plow, the saddle, and the rope.
The chuck wagon, the reata, and the brand.

questions.text: In the days of the drives many cowboys hoped to start their own herds, but by the 1880s most worked for a wage. What evidence in the lesson shows the change?

answers.text: Cowboys became the owners of the large XIT Ranch in the Panhandle.
A strike by cowboys for higher pay in 1883 failed when the owners refused.
Cowboys were paid a share of the profits from every ranch they worked.
Governor Hogg set the wages that every cowboy in Texas was to receive.

questions.text: Texas traded three million acres of Panhandle land for a new capitol, and a Chicago group turned it into the XIT Ranch. What does this show about Texas ranching?

answers.text: The state wanted ranching to stay small and local, so it refused to sell any of its land to outsiders.
Ranching had become a business that needed outside money, and a state short of cash paid in land.
The great trail drives had come to an end in the year 1866.
Only people born in Texas were allowed by law to own Texas land.

quizzes.title: Week 27 Quarter 3 Exam
quizzes.description: This exam covers Quarter 3 only, Weeks 19 to 27. Choose the best answer for each question. You have one attempt.

questions.text: Why did annexation in 1845 not settle where Texas ended in the southwest?

answers.text: Congress annexed Texas but left the exact border to be worked out with Mexico.
Mexico had already agreed that the Nueces River was the border, so only Texas disagreed about it.
Texas had no claim at all to the land along the Río Grande.
The border had been set by the treaty that was signed in 1848.

questions.text: Which result of the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo ended the argument that began the war?

answers.text: The Nueces became the border, and Texas gave up the disputed strip.
The Río Grande became the border, and Mexico gave up its claim to Texas.
The United States gave California back to Mexico in return for peace.
Texas was returned to Mexico as a province of the Mexican republic.

questions.text: At Cerro Gordo, Robert E. Lee helped win the battle. What did he do?

answers.text: He led the charge up the steep hill at the castle of Chapultepec.
He arranged the surrender of the port city of Veracruz to Scott.
He captured General Santa Anna in the field and ended the war.
He scouted the hills and found a path around the Mexican position.

questions.text: Polk let Santa Anna pass through the blockade hoping he would make peace, but Santa Anna took command of the Mexican army instead. What does this show?

answers.text: Polk wanted the war to go on for many more years, so he sent Santa Anna home on purpose.
Santa Anna was loyal to the United States and meant to help it.
The navy had never set up a blockade of the Mexican coast.
One choice, and some chance, helped create the army Scott had to fight.

questions.text: In 1850, Texas gave up claims in the west and received $10 million. How did this change Texas's finances?

answers.text: It forced Texas to leave the Union and to become independent again.
It gave Texas control over all of the land that became New Mexico.
It helped pay off debts left over from the days of the Republic.
It ended the need for the state to collect any taxes at all.

questions.text: In 1832 South Carolina tried nullification, and Jackson refused to accept it. How did the crisis end?

answers.text: A lower tariff ended the crisis, though Calhoun's idea lived on.
Jackson sent in troops and broke up the Union for good.
South Carolina left the Union that year and formed a new country.
The Supreme Court ended all tariffs and the quarrel ended with them.

questions.text: After the Dred Scott decision of 1857, many Northerners were furious and many Southerners felt safer. What did the decision say?

answers.text: Congress could not ban slavery in the territories, and Black Americans could not be citizens.
Slavery was banned in every territory of the nation by this ruling, and Black citizens won new rights.
Black Americans were declared full citizens of the nation by the Court.
Texas was told by the Court that it could never secede from the Union.

questions.text: The Secession Convention voted 166 to 8, but the later popular vote showed that some Texans voted no. What does this combination show?

answers.text: No Texans at all supported the idea of leaving the Union, and the leaders were all against it.
The popular vote was never held in any part of Texas.
Texans were not unanimous, even though their leaders were nearly so.
Every county in the state voted in exactly the same way.

questions.text: Why is the Declaration of Causes important evidence about why Texas left the Union?

answers.text: It was written by Sam Houston while he was governor, and it gave his reasons for opposing the move.
It said Texas left the Union mainly because of a new tariff.
It was kept secret from the public and was never printed.
It gave the reasons in the leaders' own words, and it named slavery again and again.

questions.text: Which fact about the 1st Texas at Antietam shows how dangerous the Texans' role in Lee's army was?

answers.text: It did not take part in the battle at Antietam at all.
It surrendered to the Union army without firing a single shot.
It lost more than 80 of every 100 men in a single day.
It lost fewer than ten men in the whole of the fight.

questions.text: Confederate cotton went through Matamoros rather than Gulf ports. What problem was this route meant to solve?

answers.text: Cotton had become too costly for Texans to grow, so they sold it only to buyers within the state.
The Union blockade made it hard to sell cotton from Confederate ports.
Mexico had banned the sale of all cotton to foreign ships.
Railroads had replaced ships for all of the trade out of Texas.

questions.text: The Battle of Palmito Ranch was fought more than a month after Lee's surrender. What can you infer about the war in the Trans-Mississippi?

answers.text: It was far from Richmond and Washington, so orders and news were slow to arrive.
The war had never really ended in Virginia, and Lee himself planned and ordered the battle in Texas.
Texas had already won the war and no longer had to fight.
Lee had planned the battle himself and ordered it from Virginia.

questions.text: Why did Congress require Texas to approve the 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments?

answers.text: They ended the draft, created public schools, and set up the Freedmen's Bureau to hand out food.
They set up the Freedmen's Bureau and paid for the public schools.
They gave women the vote and ended the poll tax in Texas.
They ended slavery, made Black Americans citizens, and protected Black men's vote.

questions.text: After Redemption in 1874, the Democratic government cut state spending and ended Davis's state police. What does this show about the new leaders' aims?

answers.text: They wanted a stronger governor with a larger police force and more power.
They wanted more federal troops to be stationed in every county.
They wanted elections to be held less often than they had been.
They wanted a smaller, cheaper government and a limit on the executive.

questions.text: Which feature of the 1876 constitution most clearly reflects fear of a strong governor?

answers.text: A four-year term and the power to appoint all of the judges.
A two-year term, a low salary, and no state police.
A state police force that took its orders from the governor.
A governor who is allowed to fire any elected state officer.

questions.text: A county commissioners court is called a court, but it is not one. What does it do?

answers.text: It hears criminal cases and decides whether the accused is guilty.
It chooses the governor and the other officers for the whole state.
It sets the county budget and tax rate and builds county roads.
It writes the laws that apply to every person in the nation.

questions.text: Which source of revenue does the state not collect?

answers.text: A sales tax.
A property tax.
Taxes on oil and gas.
Fees such as driver's licenses.

questions.text: Put the events in order: the poll tax, Smith v. Allwright, and the end of the Texas poll tax. Which sequence is correct?
Barbara Jordan won election to the U.S. House of Representatives in 1972. What was notable about this?

answers.text: She was the first Texan ever to be elected to Congress at all.
She became Speaker of the House of Representatives that same year.
She was the first Black woman from the South elected to the House.
She was elected president of the United States in the next election.

questions.text: Which fact shows how far Comanche riders could reach as late as 1840?

answers.text: They captured the capital at Austin and held it for a week.
They signed a peace with the whole of Texas at San Antonio.
They left Texas for good and moved north into Kansas.
They rode to the Gulf coast at Linnville and burned the town.

questions.text: Why did the Colt revolver change the way Rangers fought on horseback?

answers.text: It was much lighter than the bow and arrow that was used then.
It needed no ammunition of any kind in order to be fired.
It could be used only by a soldier who was standing on foot.
A rider could fire again and again without stopping to reload.

questions.text: English words such as lariat, and the practice of the dally, come from Spanish. What do they show?

answers.text: Spanish was the first language that the German settlers spoke, and they taught it to the cowboys.
The Texas cowboy inherited tools, skills, and words from the vaquero tradition.
Texans had no cattle at all in the state before the year 1850.
Cowboys first came to Texas from Europe in the middle of the 1800s.

questions.text: German Hill Country settlers smoked sausage and beef in smokehouses. What does the lesson connect this to?

answers.text: The barbecue tradition of Central Texas.
The cattle drives that went north to the railheads in Kansas.
The sale of Texas cotton to the mills of Europe.
The first Texas Ranger companies of the Republic.

questions.text: Juan Cortina said that Tejanos had lost land and been treated unjustly. How did Texas respond?

answers.text: It gave Tejano families new titles to the land they had lost, and it then asked Cortina to go home.
It signed a treaty of peace with Cortina and left him in power.
It sent Rangers under Rip Ford, who worked with U.S. soldiers to drive him across the river.
It elected Cortina governor of the state to settle the quarrel.

questions.text: Mackenzie's men shot most of the 1,400 horses captured at Palo Duro Canyon. Why was this more damaging than killing warriors would have been?

answers.text: Without horses, a Plains people could not hunt or move, and the band could not survive.
Horses were sacred to the Texans, who held that no one should kill one, even in time of war.
It broke the terms of the Medicine Lodge treaty that had just been signed.
It made the Comanche wealthy in horses and gave them new strength.

questions.text: What did Quanah Parker do after his surrender in 1875?

answers.text: He went back to the Llano Estacado and rebuilt the old bands, and led a new war against the Texans.
He joined the Texas Rangers as a scout and left the reservation.
He left no record of his life and passed from history at once.
He adapted, learning English, leasing grazing land, and speaking for his people in Washington.

questions.text: The windmill and, later, deep wells changed the plains. Which statement is supported by the lesson?

answers.text: The plains had plenty of rivers that ran all year long, so ranchers did not need windmills or deep wells at all.
Water was the big problem on the Llano Estacado, and pumping solved it, though the aquifer refills slowly.
Windmills brought more rain to the plains and ended the dry years.
The Ogallala aquifer can never run low, no matter how much is used.

questions.text: A steer worth a few dollars in Texas could bring about ten times as much in a Northern city. What does this explain?

answers.text: Why Texas banned the sale of cattle outside the state in 1866.
Why drives to railheads such as Abilene were worth the risk.
Why Kansas welcomed Texas fever and the herds that carried it.
Why the Comanche stopped raiding and took up ranching in 1867.

questions.text: Barbed wire and the windmill changed the range. Which result is described in the lesson?

answers.text: Open-range ranching became easier for the small owners in Texas, who now had more land to graze.
Cowboys became the owners of the large ranches that they had worked.
The open range closed, and ranching became a business that hired wage workers.
The legislature encouraged fence cutting as a way to protect the range.

questions.text: Why did Governor Hogg sign a law in 1891 limiting how much land foreign owners could hold?

answers.text: Texas had no land left to be sold, so the state needed a way to bring in money.
Texans worried about distant companies owning so much of the state.
The Comanche still owned the land in the Panhandle region.
The U.S. Army needed the land for building new frontier forts.

answers.text: Farmers were paid more money for every extra bale of cotton they grew.
Farmers were caught in a cycle where working harder made things worse.
Merchants refused to give any credit to farmers in the spring.
Cotton prices rose steadily every year after the year 1880.

questions.text: The Farmers' Alliance began in Lampasas County in 1877 and spread quickly. What best explains its rapid spread?

answers.text: It was started and paid for by the railroads in Texas.
Farmers in nearly every county faced the same debts and low prices.
The legislature passed a law that required every farmer to join.
It promised a free grant of land to each new member.

questions.text: The Texas Exchange, a cooperative started in 1887, ran short of money because bankers would not lend to it. What does this suggest about the farmers' position?

answers.text: Bankers were eager to help the Alliance, and they lent it large sums to build the exchange.
Cooperatives were against the law in Texas at that time.
They had little power in the banking system they were trying to work around.
Farmers had more cash on hand than the merchants who served them.

questions.text: The Colored Farmers' Alliance was a separate group from the white Alliance. What does this fact show?

answers.text: Black and white farmers shared debts and goals but were kept apart by custom.
Black farmers had no interest in farm reform, and the two groups had opposed each other's goals.
The two groups were opposed to each other's goals on every question.
Texas law required every farm club in the state to be mixed.

questions.text: The Populists backed William Jennings Bryan in 1896 and then faded. Which fact helps explain why the party lost strength in Texas?

answers.text: Bryan lost Texas by a very wide margin, and most Texans turned away from the whole idea of reform.
The Alliance voted to end the People's Party in the year 1892.
Democrats such as Hogg took up Populist ideas, and the Populists had no candidate of their own.
Texas had never had a farm movement or a farmers' club of any kind.

questions.text: Hogg took the railroads to court as attorney general and then promised a Railroad Commission as governor. How does this reform connect to the farmers' complaints?

answers.text: He joined the People's Party and led it to a great victory in the elections of 1892 across Texas.
He opposed all rules about how railroads should do their business.
He wanted foreign companies to be allowed to own more Texas land.
He turned complaints about rates and unfair treatment into law, though he was a Democrat.

questions.text: In 1918 Texas women won the vote in primary elections. Why was that so important in Texas at that time?

answers.text: The Democratic primary was the real contest, so it largely decided who won.
No other kind of election was held anywhere in the state of Texas.
Women had already won the vote in general elections as early as 1900.
Primary elections were held only to choose judges and county officers.

questions.text: Before 1900 Galveston chose not to build a seawall. Which fact from the lesson helps explain that choice?

answers.text: Federal law did not allow seawalls on the Gulf coast, and the city had no power to build one.
The island was higher than the land around it on the mainland.
Some people said the city could not be badly hurt, and the cost seemed too high.
A major storm had never before touched any part of the Gulf coast.

questions.text: The Weather Bureau did not expect the 1900 hurricane to strike Galveston. What helps explain the mistake?

answers.text: It had no weather stations along the Texas coast at all, so it could not see the storm coming.
It distrusted warnings from Cuban forecasters and expected the storm to turn toward Florida.
It had warned the people of Galveston about the storm a week earlier.
Isaac Cline was away from Galveston on the day the storm hit.

questions.text: After the storm, Galveston adopted a five-person commission to run the city, and the idea spread to hundreds of other cities. What does this show?

answers.text: The commission plan was ordered by the federal government.
Only Galveston was allowed to use the commission plan.
The city had no government at all before 1901.
A local disaster can lead to reforms that other places copy.

questions.text: The seawall held in 1915, yet Galveston never regained its old place. Which pair of facts best explains this?

answers.text: The seawall fell down in the 1915 storm, and Dallas then built a new port that took the shipping.
The railroads left the island, and Beaumont took over the cotton trade.
Insurers and banks grew nervous, and Houston's deep channel let big ships reach it directly.
The state moved the capital, and the island sank into the Gulf.

questions.text: Pattillo Higgins believed oil lay under the hill at Spindletop. What did he believe about its structure?

answers.text: That the hill was the cone of an old volcano that had once poured out the oil.
That the hill was the site of an old coal mine.
That the hill covered a trail used by the Comanche.
That the hill sat on a salt dome that trapped oil beneath it.

questions.text: The oil from Spindletop was thick and not good for lamps, yet it still became very valuable. Why?

answers.text: Lamps were no longer used in Texas, so the oil was burned only in the largest cities.
It could be turned into cotton fiber at the mills in Houston.
It burned well as fuel for trains, ships, and factories as engines spread.
The government required the army to buy it for its new trucks.

questions.text: Houston is inland on a shallow bayou. What did Houston's leaders do that Galveston's could not match?

answers.text: They persuaded the federal government to help pay for a deep channel to the city.
They moved the whole city of Houston down to the Gulf coast so that ships could reach it.
They banned all oil refining inside the limits of the city.
They built a high seawall around Buffalo Bayou to hold back storms.

questions.text: Why did East Texas oil prices crash in 1931?

answers.text: The government banned the export of all oil from the Gulf ports.
Dad Joiner closed down his wells, so supplies fell sharply.
Texas had stopped using oil in its factories and its cities.
Thousands of wells were pumping at once, which flooded the market.

questions.text: Governor Sterling sent the National Guard into the field and declared martial law. What did the drillers' behavior show?

answers.text: The state had passed no laws at all about how oil could be pumped, and the Guard was sent in anyway.
Many drillers ignored the pumping limits, and the courts had sided with them at first.
Joiner had asked the Guard to protect his wells from thieves.
The Railroad Commission had already been abolished by the legislature.

questions.text: Why did the Railroad Commission's decisions about oil affect prices around the world?

answers.text: Texas produced so much oil that the amount pumped there moved prices everywhere.
The commission owned most of the world's tanker ships, so it could decide where oil would be sold.
The commission also ran the Congress and the courts in Washington.
Texas oil was the only oil that could be found anywhere in the world.

questions.text: Kilgore grew from about 700 to about ten thousand people in a year. Why did so many workers go there during the Depression?

answers.text: The government sent them there to open new farms, and many went to work the land around the town.
Many had lost farms or jobs, and any strong worker could find a place on a drilling crew.
Kilgore had no oil, but it had very cheap land for sale.
Cotton prices had risen sharply, and farm work paid well that year.

questions.text: Dallas has no seaport or oil field. What fact best explains its early growth?

answers.text: The Trinity River carried large ships all the way to its docks, so goods could be shipped by water.
In 1872 and 1873 two railroads crossed there, making it a crossroads for cotton.
It had been the first capital of the Republic of Texas.
The Comanche chose the site as their main trading post.

questions.text: When banks failed across Texas in the Depression, Dallas banks kept growing. What helped them?

answers.text: The federal government owned and ran every one of the banks, and so it protected them from loss.
They refused to lend money to any oil company or oil driller.
Cotton prices had risen sharply across the state in those years.
Oil money from East Texas deals passed through them and gave them a cushion.

questions.text: Dallas grew from cotton, oil, banking, insurance, retail, and manufacturing at the same time. How did that help it in the Depression?

answers.text: It meant that every part of the economy failed in the same year.
It kept the Railroad Commission out of the city's business.
When one part had a bad year, the others could help carry the city.
It made the city smaller than the other large cities of Texas.

questions.text: The lesson says Texas's economy had a pattern of sudden swings. What is the best explanation it gives?

answers.text: Texans would not sell any of their goods outside the borders of the state.
Texas had too many different kinds of industry to depend on any one.
Texas sold raw goods in far-off markets and had few factories to fall back on.
Texas banks set the price of cotton and oil for the whole world.

questions.text: Tenant farmers had it worst in the Depression. Which detail supports this?

answers.text: Tenant farmers owned the land that they worked on.
Tenants received federal pensions as early as 1930.
Landowners sent families away or cut their pay.
Cotton prices were rising in the early years of the 1930s.

questions.text: The dust storms of the 1930s struck the High Plains especially hard. Which two facts together best explain why?

answers.text: Farmers had plowed up the grass that held the soil, and the rain stopped.
Gulf winds changed direction, and the railroads shut down for years.
Oil wells ran dry, and the farmers sold off all of their cattle.
Hurricanes struck far inland, and the rivers flooded the wheat fields.

questions.text: Why did the state government of Texas offer so little relief at first?

answers.text: The governor refused to meet with the legislature during those years, so no relief law could ever be passed.
The 1876 constitution limited spending and borrowing, and Texans did not look to government for help.
Federal law forbade the states from giving any kind of relief at all.
Texas had no money problems at all during the years of the Depression.

questions.text: Radio created a new kind of culture. What was new about it?

answers.text: Radio could be heard only in the largest cities, which were the only places with electric power.
Millions of people in many places heard the same songs, shows, and news at once.
Radio replaced all of the newspapers in Texas right away.
Each Texas town could hear only its own small local station.

questions.text: The New Deal changed federalism in Texas. How did it get around the limits of the 1876 constitution?

answers.text: It rewrote the constitution of Texas so that the state could spend more.
It abolished the Texas legislature for the years of the Depression.
It made Texas a territory of the United States once again.
Washington could spend money where the state could not or would not.

questions.text: Most rural Texas homes had no electricity before the Rural Electrification Administration. Why not?

answers.text: Texans did not want electricity in their homes, so the companies never tried to sell it to them.
There were no power plants anywhere in the state of Texas.
Private companies did not think it paid to string wires across thin country.
The state had banned all electric lines in the countryside by law.

questions.text: Doris Miller was a cook on the West Virginia, and the Navy did not let Black sailors serve in fighting jobs. What does his action at Pearl Harbor show?

answers.text: The Navy had trained him as a gunner before the war began.
The Navy had already ended all of its barriers by that time.
He was serving at the time as one of the ship's officers.
He acted with courage far beyond the job the Navy had given him.

questions.text: Why was Texas a good place to train soldiers and pilots?

answers.text: It had no large cities in the way, and the army found it easy to build camps there.
It had good weather, open land, and the support of Texas congressmen.
It had no enemies of any kind anywhere in the region nearby.
It had the only airfields in the whole country at that time.

questions.text: The government built the Big Inch and Little Big Inch pipelines. What problem did they solve?

answers.text: Texas had no oil that could be shipped to the East Coast, so the government had to build the lines.
Trains could not carry any fuel of any kind across the country.
German submarines were sinking tankers along the coast, so shipping oil by sea was dangerous.
The East Coast refused to buy any oil that came from Texas.

questions.text: Crystal City held families of Japanese, German, and Italian descent, including some American citizens. What does this show about the war?

answers.text: All of the families were soldiers in training.
The camp was used as a site for exchanging prisoners.
The war had a hard side, even far from the battlefield.
The families went there to take part in training.

questions.text: Soldiers from Texas trained and fought beside soldiers from every other state. What effect did the lesson say this had?

answers.text: Many later said it made them feel American, while they still thought of themselves as Texans.
It made many Texans stop thinking of themselves as Texans, and most of them chose to leave the state.
It had no effect on how they saw themselves or their country.
It made them much less willing to leave Texas to see the world.

questions.text: Mexico refused to send braceros to Texas for several years. What reason does the lesson give?

answers.text: How Mexican Americans and Mexican workers had been treated in Texas.
Texas had no farms that needed any workers, so Mexico saw no reason to send them there.
Mexico needed all of its own workers to stay at home.
Texas had not asked to be a part of the program.

questions.text: The lesson says the change toward national life was not something that had to happen. Which statement fits this view?

answers.text: It was caused only by the Great Depression, and the war had nothing at all to do with it in the end.
It was planned by Texas leaders in the year 1900 and carried out.
It came from decisions by Texans and by Washington, along with a war that left no other choice.
It happened because Texans wanted to leave the Union once more.

questions.text: Which combination best explains why mass growth in the Sunbelt became possible after World War II?

answers.text: Air conditioning that made summers livable, along with cheap land and low taxes.
Cooler summers across the whole state, along with higher taxes on every business that came to Texas.
The end of the oil industry, along with the closing of the bases.
Higher rainfall across the plains, along with the creation of new rivers.

questions.text: In 1940 most Texans lived on farms and in small towns, and by 1950 more lived in cities. What does this show?

answers.text: Texas changed from a mostly rural state to an urban one within a decade.
Texas had fewer people living in the state in 1950 than it had had in the year 1940.
The cities of Texas had stopped growing and had begun to shrink.
Farming came to an end in the state of Texas after the war.

questions.text: San Antonio grew more slowly and with less wealth than Houston or Dallas. Which strength does the lesson give for San Antonio?

answers.text: Oil refineries along a deep channel that led to the Gulf of Mexico.
Aircraft factories that employed many thousands of workers in the city.
The military bases, along with its history and its Mexican American culture.
A deep-water port on the Gulf that was open to ocean ships.

questions.text: Why did the University of Texas and Texas A&M have a special advantage when they grew after the war?

answers.text: The federal government paid all of their costs for many decades, so they never needed any other money.
They charged no fees at all to students who came from other states.
Public land in West Texas set aside for them earned large sums when oil was found there.
They received a share of the money earned by Houston's medical center.

questions.text: Why did the Supreme Court rule in Sweatt v. Painter that the separate law school was not equal?

answers.text: It was too far away from the city of Houston for most students, and it had no real library.
It had too many students for the few rooms that it was given.
It cost far more to attend than the University of Texas Law School.
It could not give the same education, with the same teachers, library, and standing.

questions.text: The GI Forum took up the case of Felix Longoria. What did the case show?

answers.text: The Forum could change the laws of Texas on its own authority, and it did so after the Longoria case.
The army refused to bury any soldiers who were killed overseas.
A soldier killed in the war could still be refused a funeral because he was Mexican American.
Longoria had asked for a separate cemetery for Mexican American soldiers.

questions.text: Hernandez v. Texas reached the Supreme Court in 1954. What did the Court decide?

answers.text: Only white and Black people were protected by the Fourteenth Amendment, so Mexican Americans had no claim.
The Constitution protects Mexican Americans from being kept off juries because of their background.
Every Texas jury from then on had to include a Mexican American member.
Pete Hernandez had to go free because the Court found that he was innocent.

questions.text: Why did American computer companies form the MCC in 1983?

answers.text: The federal government ordered them to merge into one company that would be run by the army.
They wanted to move their factories to Mexico to cut their costs.
The University of Texas needed money from them to build new labs.
They worried that Japan's plan for new computers would let it take the lead.

questions.text: Austin won MCC over cities such as Atlanta and San Diego. What helped it win?

answers.text: Austin already had more computer factories than any rival city, so it won without making any offer.
The University of Texas, the governor, and local leaders joined to make an offer.
Austin had a seaport where large ships could dock and unload goods.
Austin was at that time the capital of the whole United States.

questions.text: MCC's research had mixed success. Why does the lesson still say it mattered to Austin?

answers.text: It beat Japan's computer project and won the race outright.
The people it brought stayed, and some started new companies.
It built the city's main airport and its largest highway.
It made Dell Computer into an agency of the Texas government.

questions.text: In 2000 and 2001, many Austin internet companies failed, and the industry recovered. What does this suggest about Austin's tech sector?

answers.text: Technology companies never fail when they are located in a college town, and Austin's firms did not fail.
Austin had no tech workers left in the city after the year 2001.
A city built on a new industry must be ready for swings, but skilled workers helped it recover.
The University closed its engineering school after the internet bust ended.

questions.text: Audiences at the Armadillo included college students, hippies, and ranchers. What does this show about Austin's music scene?

answers.text: It kept students out of its shows and played only for adults who came from other parts of the state.
It played only classical music in the old armory building at night.
It crossed lines between rock fans and country fans that kept other Texas scenes apart.
It was run by the big Nashville studios and sent its profits there.

questions.text: Austin City Limits began regular broadcasts in 1975. How did it help Austin's music?

answers.text: It showed viewers across the country what was happening in Austin.
It put an end to outlaw country music in the state and sent its singers back to Nashville.
It kept the local bands from ever going out on tour.
It was shown only inside the city limits of Austin.

questions.text: Why do students play such a large part in Austin's live-music scene?

answers.text: The university bans musicians from performing on or near its campus.
Tens of thousands of undergraduates make a ready audience on any night.
Students are paid by the city to play at all of the clubs.
The state forbids bands from touring anywhere outside of Austin.

questions.text: After the Bracero Program ended in 1964, the number of immigrants without legal papers rose. Which fact best explains this?

answers.text: Mexico stopped allowing anyone at all to leave the country for work, so the farm program simply ended.
Farmers no longer needed any workers because machines did all the work.
Texas banned all farm work for people who were born outside the state.
Farmers still wanted workers and workers wanted jobs, but a legal way to come was gone for many.

questions.text: How did maquiladoras tie the border economies together?

answers.text: They sold large tracts of land in Texas to Mexican companies, who built farms and homes on it.
They assembled goods in Mexico from American parts and sent the finished goods back.
They taught English in the public schools of northern Mexico.
They built the dams along the Rio Grande to supply water.

questions.text: The lesson says supporters and critics of NAFTA both found evidence for their views. What does this suggest?

answers.text: NAFTA had no effect on the trade among the three countries, so nothing changed after it began.
All economists agreed from the start that the agreement was a failure.
The effects of the agreement were mixed, and people weighed them differently.
Only Texans were affected by the agreement, and no one else.

questions.text: Thousands of families live in colonias that often lack paved roads and clean water. What does this show about border growth?

answers.text: The border has no families living on it today.
Growth did not reach everyone.
The government has already solved all of these problems.
Growth along the border stopped during the 1980s.

questions.text: John Tower's win in 1961 was the first Republican victory for a Texas Senate seat since Reconstruction. What did it suggest?

answers.text: That Texans might be willing to vote for a Republican.
That Democrats had left Texas for good and would never win another race.
That Lyndon Johnson had joined the Republicans.
That the Senate seat had been abolished.

questions.text: In 1970 Lloyd Bentsen beat Ralph Yarborough in the Democratic primary. What does this show about Texas Democrats?

answers.text: Conservative and liberal Democrats competed inside the same party.
Republicans had won the Democratic party's primary election outright.
Texas no longer had any Democrats left in the state.
Yarborough was a very conservative member of the Democratic party.

questions.text: Some historians argue that the Republican turn was "an old Texas outlook finding a new party." Which fact from the lesson supports that view?

answers.text: Texas had always voted for Republican candidates in every election, and never for any Democrat.
Texans had no opinion at all about taxes or about spending.
Texas leaders had never paid any attention to what Washington did.
Texas had a long tradition of self-reliance and distrust of distant government.

questions.text: The Texas electric grid is mostly separate from the national grids. Which statement best fits the lesson?

answers.text: It is run directly by the federal government in Washington, which sets its rules and prices each year.
It was built for the first time after the winter storm of 2021.
It ties Texas closely to the grids of every other state.
It is mostly free from federal oversight, but it cannot easily borrow power from other states.

questions.text: Which change in the 1930s helped bring Texas closer to the rest of the nation?

answers.text: The closing of the Rio Grande border to all trade and travel, which ended the Mexican trade.
The New Deal, which brought federal jobs, electricity, and farm programs.
The end of the oil industry and the loss of its jobs.
The creation of a separate Texas currency and Texas banks.

questions.text: Which of these is an example of divergence after about 1970?

answers.text: Texas voters turned toward the Republican Party and a smaller role for Washington.
Texans joined the national draft for the first time in their history, and so became more alike.
Radio reached nearly every Texas town and farm by the 1930s.
Texas stopped trading with Mexico and with the other states.

questions.text: The Rio Grande water treaty of 1944 has become a source of tension in droughts. Why?

answers.text: The river dried up completely in the year 1944 and never returned.
The treaty banned all farming along both banks of the river.
It is a shared resource, and droughts make both sides want more of it.
Mexico refused to sign the treaty, and Texas ignored it.

questions.text: Texas is the nation's biggest exporter, and Mexico is its biggest customer. What does this show about the border?

answers.text: The border is closed to trade of every kind and for everyone.
Mexico buys almost nothing that is made or grown in Texas.
Trade has tied the Texas and Mexican economies closely together.
Texas depends mainly on its trade with Canada and with Europe.

questions.text: Which statement best sums up the lesson's answer to whether Texas is just another American state?

answers.text: Texas is deeply part of the nation and still has its own identity.
Texas is exactly like every other state in the whole country.
Texas is completely separate from the nation in every respect.
Texas stopped being distinct from other states around the year 1900.

questions.text: A farmer needed money months before the crop came in, so he bought goods on credit from a merchant who took a claim on the crop. What is this called?

answers.text: A crop lien.
A cooperative.
A homestead.
A bond.

questions.text: Why does the Lampasas County origin of the Farmers' Alliance matter?

answers.text: It was one of the places where a national farm protest movement began.
It was the first capital of the Republic of Texas for a time.
It was the first railroad town to be built in the whole state.
It was the site of the last Populist convention before the party ended.

questions.text: Which statement best explains why the Populist Party declined after 1896?

answers.text: Cotton prices doubled, and the farmers lost their reasons to protest against the railroads.
Texas passed a law that outlawed all of the political parties.
Its members had backed a Democrat, and Democrats took up some of its ideas.
The Alliance voted to break up the party after its defeat in 1896.

questions.text: What was the Railroad Commission created in 1891 to do?

answers.text: To build new railroads for the state with public money.
To run the Texas Rangers on the frontier in the 1890s.
To oversee railroads and set the rates they could charge.
To collect taxes from the farmers who lived along the rail lines.

questions.text: Why did the Democratic primary matter so much for women's suffrage in Texas?

answers.text: Primaries were open only to women voters, which let them choose all of the candidates for every office.
Winning the primary vote in 1918 let women vote in the real contest, before the national amendment.
Primaries had been ended by the legislature before the year 1918.
The primary was run by the Congress and not by the state of Texas.

questions.text: Which fact best explains why the 1900 hurricane killed so many people in Galveston?

answers.text: The island sat on top of a tall hill that the sea could not reach, and the city was well prepared.
There were very few people living on the island in the year 1900.
The island was low, a surge of about fifteen feet covered it, and many had not left.
The storm struck the island with no wind and only a little rain.

questions.text: Which was part of Galveston's rebuilding?

answers.text: A concrete seawall and raising the ground with sand pumped from the harbor.
A new capitol building for the state in the middle of the island, built after the storm.
A ban on ships using the harbor and a new set of port laws.
A plan to move the whole city to higher land near Houston.

questions.text: What did Anthony Lucas need that Pattillo Higgins lacked before the Spindletop gusher?

answers.text: A mining permit that had to be signed by Congress.
A railroad line that ran from the hill into the town.
More money, which he found from bankers in Pittsburgh.
A partner who was chosen from among the Comanche people.

questions.text: What did the Houston Ship Channel make possible?

answers.text: Houston became a seaside resort for tourists who came from Dallas, and it grew a large new beach front.
Galveston became the new capital of Texas after the storm of 1900.
Cattle drives became much easier to organize across the Brazos River.
Ocean ships could sail up to the city's docks, and Houston became a refining and shipping center.

questions.text: What was Dad Joiner's discovery in October 1930?

answers.text: A well that proved to be the first of an enormous oil field in East Texas.
A coal mine under the streets of the city of Dallas, which became the center of the coal trade.
A great gusher on the hill called Spindletop near Beaumont.
A buried Spanish mission in the pine woods of Rusk County.

questions.text: What was the purpose of proration?

answers.text: To raise taxes on the gasoline stations of the whole state and to pay for the new state roads.
To make all oil drilling against the law in East Texas.
To build more pipelines across the state to the East Coast.
To limit how much oil each well could pump, so prices and pressure would not be ruined.

questions.text: Why did Dallas grow into a city of commerce even though it had no seaport?

answers.text: It sat on the shore of the Gulf of Mexico, and ocean ships brought cotton to its docks.
Railroads crossed there, and its banks and insurers served nearby industries.
It had the largest oil field in the whole of the world.
The army made it the capital city of the state of Texas.

questions.text: Which statement best describes the effect of the Great Depression on Texas farmers?

answers.text: Cotton prices rose sharply, and the farmers grew richer each year than they had been before.
Cotton fell below the cost of growing it, and many lost land or became tenants.
Farmers moved to the cities and ran the banks that failed there.
Farmers refused to plant any crops at all through the whole decade.

questions.text: Why did the Texas state government offer little relief at first?

answers.text: Its constitution limited spending and borrowing, and Texans did not look to government for help.
It had no governor in office at any time during those years, and no one in Austin could ask for aid.
Federal law forbade the state from giving any relief to its people.
Its income tax was too high for the state to raise any more.

questions.text: The Rural Electrification Administration lent money to local cooperatives. What did that do?

answers.text: It built new highways that crossed the whole of the state and linked the farms to the towns.
It brought electric lines to farms that private companies had passed over.
It paid farmers to stop growing cotton on their poorest fields.
It set up the first radio stations in the cities of Texas.

questions.text: Texans listened to the same radio programs as people in Georgia and Ohio. What does this show about Texas in the 1930s?

answers.text: A national mass culture was beginning to reach Texas.
Texas had banned all of the national radio programs.
Radio had no effect on the way of life in Texas.
Texans refused to listen to music of any kind.

questions.text: Why were shipyards on the Gulf Coast and aircraft plants in Fort Worth and Dallas important to the war?

answers.text: They supplied the Confederate army with its guns and its food during the whole of the long war.
They built ships and bombers and brought many workers, including women, into new jobs.
They guarded the long Mexican border against raids and smugglers.
They took over the work that had been done by the Railroad Commission.

questions.text: Why did Mexico keep braceros out of Texas at first?

answers.text: Because of how Mexican workers and Mexican Americans were treated in Texas.
Because Texas had no farms that needed any extra workers, and so did not ask for any of them.
Because Mexico needed all of those workers to stay at home.
Because Texas had chosen to run its own separate program.

questions.text: Many historians call World War II the completion of the "Americanization of Texas." Which fact supports this?

answers.text: Texas rejoined the country of Mexico after the war was over, and all Texans became citizens of Mexico.
Texans gave up speaking English and spoke only in Spanish.
Texas left the Union a second time when the war was won.
Texans served in the same army, paid the same taxes, and read the same news as other Americans.

questions.text: Which pair of facts best explains why Texas became an urban Sunbelt state after the war?

answers.text: Cold winters drove people south, and cotton prices were high, so farm families moved to the cities.
Rivers dried up, and the oil industry was banned by law.
Air conditioning made summers livable, and cheap land and jobs drew workers.
New railroads opened, and the army grew far larger in size.

questions.text: What did the Supreme Court rule in Sweatt v. Painter?

answers.text: Black students could not be allowed to attend any law school, and Sweatt had to leave Texas.
The hurried separate law school was not equal, and Sweatt had to be admitted.
The University of Texas had to close its law school for good.
Texas had to end segregation in all of its public schools at once.

questions.text: Which group was founded in 1948 to defend the rights of Mexican American veterans?

answers.text: LULAC.
The Populist Party.
The Texas Equal Rights Association.
The American G.I. Forum.

questions.text: Why did American technology companies form the MCC?

answers.text: To compete with the Texas oil industry for workers and money.
To build a new seaport for the state on the Gulf coast.
To train new recruits for the Texas Rangers in Austin.
To answer Japan's plan for new computers by sharing research.

questions.text: What helped make Austin a city of live music?

answers.text: A seaport and a number of large factories along the river that brought in many workers.
The Armadillo, Austin City Limits, SXSW, and a large student audience.
A government ban on all concerts held in the city limits.
A lack of any colleges or universities within the whole city.

questions.text: What were maquiladoras?

answers.text: Cattle ranches in South Texas that raised longhorn cattle for the markets of the North.
Army forts that were built along the Rio Grande in the 1800s.
Factories in Mexico, often near the border, that assemble goods for export.
Oil refineries on the Gulf Coast near Houston and Beaumont.

questions.text: Which statement best describes NAFTA as the lesson tells it?

answers.text: It created one single government to rule all of North America, and ended the old national borders.
It removed most tariffs among three countries, and both sides found evidence for their views.
It ended all of the trade between Texas and the country of Mexico.
It made the state of Texas leave the Union for a second time.

questions.text: Which sequence shows how Texas politics changed?

answers.text: Reagan lost Texas in 1980, and Tower did not win until 1998 when he beat the governor then in office.
Republicans won every statewide office in the year 1961, with Tower.
Democrats won every statewide office in Texas after the year 1998.
Tower won in 1961, Reagan carried Texas in 1980, and Republicans swept every office in 1998.

questions.text: Which of the following is an example of Texas diverging from the nation after about 1970?

answers.text: The national draft that began before the war and took many of the young men from Texas.
The New Deal programs of the 1930s that brought federal money and jobs into Texas towns.
The national radio programs that were heard in every town across the whole country.
Its own electric grid, run separately from the large national grids.
